case_name: 1216393 Ontario Inc. v Parabellum Law Corporation
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

1216393 Ontario Inc. v. Parabellum Law
Corporation,

2017 BCSC 1223

Date: 20170505

Docket:
114108

Registry: Kelowna

Between:

1216393
Ontario Inc., Tylon Steepe Homes Ltd.

and
Dennis Kretschmer

Plaintiffs

And

Parabellum
Law Corporation

Defendant

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice G.P. Weatherill

Oral Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

Appearing on his own behalf and on behalf
of all Plaintiffs:

D.
Kretschmer

Counsel for the Defendants:

J.C.
MacInnis

Place and Date of Hearing:

Kelowna,
B.C.

May
5, 2017

Place and Date of Ruling:

Kelowna,
B.C.

May
5, 2017

[
1
]

THE COURT:
This
is an application for security for costs to be posted by the plaintiffs. The
plaintiffs sued the defendant law corporation for damages for professional
negligence some five and a half years after the termination of the parties'
solicitor/client relationship. The defendant is owned and operated by Mr. Stephen
Turner, lawyer, who in separate proceedings claims in excess of $200,000 from
the plaintiffs for unpaid legal fees.

[
2
]

The plaintiff Mr. Kretschmer is a principal
of the two corporate plaintiffs 1216393 Ontario Inc. (“121”) and Tylon Steepe
Homes Ltd. (“Tylon”).

[
3
]

The plaintiffs were involved in a series of
lawsuits between 2005 and 2011 arising out of a subdivision development on
Kalamalka Lake, north of Kelowna, B.C., known as Crystal Waters. That
development started in the 1999 timeframe.

[
4
]

The focus of the plaintiffs' complaint against Mr. Turner
starts in 2009 when the plaintiffs retained him in connection with a legal-fee
review respecting one of the plaintiffs' former lawyers, Mr. Rotstein.

Background

[
5
]

The history of the Crystal Waters development
and various lawsuits that arose out of it is long and complicated. It has been described
at length in a number of decisions both in this Court and in the Court of
Appeal. The details need not be recited here. It is fair to say that the entire
affair has been expensive and unpleasant for the plaintiffs, who were unsuccessful
in most every respect.

[
6
]

However, a brief summary would be helpful to put
my decision in perspective. The story begins in the 2002-2003 timeframe and
involves what was referred to as “First-Tier” purchasers (“Original
Purchasers”) entering into contracts with 121 for the purchase of strata lots
at Crystal Waters (“First Purchase Contracts”). Mr. Kretschmer put the
Purchase Contracts together on behalf of 121. Tylon was to be the home building
contractor for the Original Purchasers.

[
7
]

In 2005 while the subdivision was being
developed, 121 terminated the First Purchase Contracts seeking instead to
re-sell the properties to other purchasers, referred to as the “Second-Tier”
Purchasers, for more money.

[
8
]

121 then entered into binding contracts to sell
the same lots to the Second-Tier Purchasers (“Second Purchase Contracts”).

[
9
]

A number of the Original Purchasers sued
claiming specific performance of the First Purchase Contracts.

[
10
]

One of those actions, known as the “Romfo”
action was heard by Mr. Justice Myers in September 2007. Judgment was
granted in favour of the Romfo plaintiffs and specific performance of the First
Purchase Contracts was ordered. The plaintiffs’ then lawyer, Mr. Rotstein,
was counsel representing them in the Romfo trial.

[
11
]

As a result of the Romfo decision, 121 could not
complete on the Second Purchase Contracts and some of the Second-Tier
Purchasers also sued.

[
12
]

The Romfo matter was appealed and in April 2008,
the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. Mr. Rotstein was counsel on that
appeal.

[
13
]

In November 2010, Mr. Turner took over as
counsel of record in what has been called the “Roy” and the “Landon” actions
involving Second Purchase Contracts. Mr. Turner also assisted another of
the plaintiffs’ lawyers, Mr. Le Dressay, in a related Second Purchase
Contract action known as the “Pont” action.

[
14
]

Mr. Turner also represented the plaintiffs
in a legal-fee review hearing against Mr. Rotstein's account. That review
took place in December 2010.

[
15
]

The Rotstein fee-review hearing was successful
for the plaintiffs and funds in the order of $108,000 were ordered to be repaid
by Mr. Rotstein. Those funds are currently being held in Mr. Turner’s
trust account. Mr. Turner is claiming a solicitor's lien over those funds
because he alleges has over $200,000 in legal fees outstanding.

[
16
]

In April 2011, Justice Josephson heard the Roy
action. While he found 121 liable for damages to the plaintiffs, he dismissed
the claim against Mr. Kretschmer personally.

[
17
]

Also in the April 2011 timeframe, the Landon and
Pont actions settled. The plaintiffs say this was because of poor preparation,
poor advice and other misdeeds by Mr. Turner. These allegations against Mr. Turner
are part of this lawsuit.

[
18
]

In June 2011, the solicitor/client relationship
between the plaintiffs and the defendant ceased and Mr. Turner commenced a
fee-review hearing.

[
19
]

In December 2011, the Court of Appeal heard the
appeal of Mr. Justice Josephson's decision in the Roy action. The Court of
Appeal remitted the matter back for a new trial on all issues. Mr. Le Dressay
was the plaintiffs’ counsel on that appeal.

[
20
]

In November 2012, the second trial of the Roy
action took place before Madam Justice Bruce, who granted judgment against Mr. Kretschmer
personally but dismissed the claim against 121. It is of note that the finding
by Madam Justice Bruce against Mr. Kretschmer was for fraudulent
misrepresentation. Madam Justice Bruce's decision was then appealed, and in
November 2014, the Court of Appeal upheld the finding of fraudulent
misrepresentation against Mr. Kretschmer and further allowed the appeal against
121. The Court of Appeal found 121 liable for damages in an amount to be
assessed.

[
21
]

Meanwhile, the defendant’s fee review progressed
through the courts, albeit at a very slow pace. The fee review has still not
been finalized. It was set for a nine‑day hearing to commence
February 6, 2017, but on January 31, 2017, the plaintiffs commenced this action,
the result being that the nine‑day fee-review hearing was adjourned
generally. Mr. Kretschmer tells me that it is adjourned until the
determination of this case.

[
22
]

On that backdrop, the defendant brings this
application for security for costs. The principles involved in determining
whether an order should be granted for security for costs are well known. The
defendant relies on a series of cases respecting the considerations for
security for costs orders against corporations, including
Kropp v. Swaneset
Bay Golf Course Ltd.
,
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, [1997] B.C.J. No. 593 [
Kropp
];
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160
[
Citizens
]; and
Fat Mel's Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield
Insurance Co.
,
1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, [1993] 25 BCAC 95 [
Fat Mel’s
].

[
23
]

These cases set out the considerations and
principles that can be summarized as set out in paragraph 17 of
Kropp
:

1. The court has a complete discretion
whether to order security, and will act in light of all the relevant
circumstances;

2. The possibility or probability that the
plaintiff company will be deterred from pursuing its claim is not without more
sufficient reason for not ordering security;

3. The court must attempt to balance
injustices arising from use of security as an instrument of oppression to
stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of impecuniosity as a means
of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the other;

4. The court may have regard to the merits
of the action, but should avoid going into detail on the merits unless success
or failure appears obvious;

5. The court can order any amount of
security up to the full amount claimed, as long as the amount is more than
nominal;

6. Before the court refuses to order
security on the ground that it would unfairly stifle a valid claim, the court
must be satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it is probable that the claim
would be stifled;

7. The lateness
of the application for security is a circumstance which can properly be taken
into account.

[
24
]

At paragraph 22 the court states:

To succeed in
showing that an order for security would stifle the action the plaintiff must
do more than show that it has no assets:  See
Paul v. General Magnaplate
Corp.
(1995),
1995 CanLII 7259 (ON CTGD)
, 27 O.R. (3d) 314 (Gen.Div.). The defendants have already made
out a
prima facie
case that the corporate plaintiff has insufficient
assets to pay costs if unsuccessful. Mr. Kropp's affidavit does not really
add to that position and establish that the corporate plaintiff is impecunious,
in the sense of lacking any means of raising money for security. I think the
law requires him to do so. As Megarry, V.C., said in
Pearson
, supra, at
535, the purpose of the provision is to protect "the community against
litigious abuses by artificial persons manipulated by natural persons."

[
25
]

At paragraph 24:

So I am
respectfully of the view that the learned chambers judge erred in finding that
the corporate plaintiff would be prevented from pursuing its claim if security
were to be ordered. And it would, in my view, be contrary to the principles
enunciated above to refuse security on the grounds that the corporate plaintiff
would "have difficulty" in pursuing the action if security for costs
were to be ordered. It seems likely, as the defendants contend, that the
learned chambers judge failed adequately to distinguish between the position of
Mr. Kropp as a natural person, and the corporate plaintiff as an artificial
legal entity. I think this is entirely understandable, given the failure to
distinguish in the statement of claim between the claims of the two plaintiffs.

[
26
]

In the
Citizens
case, Justice Romilly
stated at paras. 22, 23 and 24:

22.       To succeed in showing that an
order for security would stifle the action, the plaintiff must show that it has
insufficient assets and no means of raising money for security:
Kropp,
supra
. In the case at bar, there is [a] dearth [of] evidence as to the
financial state of affairs of the plaintiff. There is also a dearth of evidence
as to any access the plaintiff may have to resources. Consequently, though it
appears that the plaintiff may be unable to pay costs of the action, it does
not follow, in the absence of evidence
that such a state of affairs would
result in stifling the advancement of the plaintiff’s claim if costs were
ordered to be secured
.

23.       In sum, on an application for
security for costs, once the defendants have established a prima facie case
that the plaintiff lacks exigible assets, the plaintiff is required to respond
with evidence to establish either that it will be able to pay the defendants'
costs, that the defendants have no arguable case, or that an order for security
will stifle the action. These tests serve to balance the possible injustice of
stifling the corporate plaintiff’s claim against the possible injustices of
exposing the defendants to a law suit where they could not recover their costs
if successful.

24.       An additional factor that might
guide the exercise of the court’s discretion in ordering security for costs is
the status of the plaintiff’s residence as a reciprocating state. …

[Emphasis added]

[
27
]

Finally, in the Court of Appeal decision in
Fat
Mel's
, at paragraph
16
, the court stated:

16.       The making of an order under
s. 229 of the
Company Act
is discretionary. However, once the
applicant for security has shown that the plaintiff will not be able to pay
costs should the claim fail, security is generally ordered unless the court is
satisfied that there is no arguable defence. …

…

28.       Master Joyce in
3473 Investment
Ltd. v. Orr
(22 May 1991), Vancouver C916920 (B.C.S.C.), made the following
statement:

In my opinion the impecuniosity of the
plaintiff company, which is the very foundation of the defendants' application,
cannot be used to defeat its entitlement to security. It appears to me that the
plaintiff or its principals or investors or backers seek to retain the
protection of the corporate veil in avoiding any exposure to costs while
maintaining the action in the hope of recovering damages. They seek a win‑win
position. I am of the view they are not entitled to do so. I am simply not
persuaded that if security is ordered the plaintiff will not be able to
prosecute the claim.

[
28
]

The defendant also refers to a series of cases
dealing with the court's discretion to order security for costs against
individual plaintiffs. For example,
I.J. v. J.A.M.
,
2013 BCSC 270
[
I.J.
v. J.A.M.
]; and
Tresoro Mining Corporation v. Mercer Gold Corp. (B.C.)
,

2015 BCSC 1822
[
Tresoro
].

[
29
]

Both of those decisions are instructive. I refer
to the comments of Justice Burnyeat in
I.J. v. J.A.M.

Starting at
paragraph
10
:

10.       The Court has the inherent
jurisdiction to order security for costs. Whether security is to be awarded is
within the discretion of the Court:
Launer v. Sommerfeld
,
1964 CanLII 444 (BC SC)
, [1964] 45
D.L.R. (2d) 293; and
Pomerleau v. Thorpe
,
[2009] B.C.J. No. 722
(S.C.)
. In this regard, there is no rule of Court in British Columbia governing
when an order for security for costs should be made against an individual:
Han
v. Cho
,
2008 BCSC 1229
, 62 C.P.C. (6th) 235 (B.C.S.C.).

11.       In the case of a personal
defendant, Ehrcke J. in
Beasse v. Holness
,
2006 BCSC 1265 (CanLII)
, [2006] B.C.J. No. 1928
(S.C.), stated:

In the case of a personal plaintiff, the
basic rule is that a natural person should not be barred from having his day in
court because of poverty and therefore the power to require the posting of
security of costs should be exercised with restraint. An order should not be
made without good reason.

12.       It is clear that the power to make
an order should be:  "... exercised cautiously, sparingly and indeed under
very special circumstances":
Tordoff v. Canada Life Assurance Co.

(1985)
1985 CanLII 492 (BC SC)
, 64 B.C.L.R. 46 (S.C.), at para.
14
;
Falso v. DeStefanis,

[1992] B.C.J. No. 337
;
Fraser v. Houston
(1997)
1997 CanLII 3227 (BC SC)
, 36 B.C.L.R. (3d)
118 (S.C.), at paras.
5 and 10
;
Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc.

(2001),
2001 BCSC 1208 (CanLII)
, 10 C.P.C. (5th) 148 (B.C.S.C.), at para.
20
;
Wong v. Huang
,

2004 BCSC 848 (CanLII)
, [2004] B.C.J. No. 1302 (S.C.), at para.
32
. In
Fraser
, supra
,
it was stated that orders should not be made except in egregious circumstances
amounting to an abuse of the court’s jurisdiction.

…

14.       A
number of factors have been considered by the Court in determining whether it
is appropriate to make an order for security costs against an individual
claimant:  (a) the merits of the plaintiff’s claim:
Tordoff
, supra
, at paras.
19‑20
;
F
rank Hillis Logging Co. v. Hoeya Sound Logging Ltd.
,
1968 CanLII 1036 (BC CA)
, [1971] 2 W.W.R.
471 (B.C.C.A.); and
Launer, supra
;
Mobilificio Trebbianco, S.p.A. v.
Rome
,
[1981] B.C.J. No. 374 (S.C.)
; (b) the inability of defendants to
recover costs from a plaintiff such as where the plaintiff is bankrupt or
insolvent:
Han
, supra
, at para.
16
; (c) whether the plaintiff has
demonstrated an intention not to comply with previous orders relating to costs
payable; (d) if there is a risk that the plaintiff is not
"findable":
Han
, supra
, at para.
17
; and (e) where there
was evidence suggesting that a false description of residence or a false name
had been given to the court or used generally:
Fraser v. Palmer
(1883),
3 Y.&C. Ex. 279; and
Swanzy v. Swanzy
(1858), 4 K.& J. 237.

[
30
]

At paragraph 16:

16.       The
onus is on [the defendant in this case] to show that this order should be made.
…

[
31
]

Continuing at paragraph 23:

23.       In Island Research &
Development Corp. v. The Boeing Co.,
1991 CanLII 598 (BC SC)
, [1991] B.C.J. No. 12 (S.C.), Spencer
J. stated:

The factors to be considered in achieving a
just balance between the defendants' right to protection and the plaintiffs'
right to advance a potential claim for adjudication include the chance of the
claim’s success, the anticipated level of cost in conducting the action and the
prospect of the plaintiffs ever having assets from which to pay the defendants'
costs if the claim fails.

[
32
]

The same considerations and factors are set out
in the
Tresoro
Mining Corporation
case at paragraphs 19, 21, 28 and 36. At
para. 41, Justice Fenlon quoted from the
Han v. Cho
,
2008 BCSC
1229
, decision of Madam Justice Dillon as follows:

The power to
order security for costs against an individual is to be exercised cautiously,
sparingly, and only under special circumstances, sometimes described as
egregious circumstances. Such special circumstances could arise if an
impecunious plaintiff also has a weak claim, or has failed to pay costs before,
or refused to follow a court order for payment of maintenance.

[
33
]

I pause to note a claim by the Canada Revenue
Agency against the plaintiff Mr. Kretschmer for outstanding income taxes
is in the $80,000 range. That judgment has been registered against his quarter
interest in the only property it appears that he owns, certainly in this
jurisdiction.

[
34
]

In exercising my discretion to order security
for costs against an individual plaintiff, I can take into account the merits
of the plaintiff's claim against Mr. Turner's corporation which appear to
me to be weak.

[
35
]

For substantially the reasons set out in the
defendant’s notice of application as expounded in Mr. MacInnis’
submissions, I am easily satisfied that an order for security for costs should
be made by the plaintiffs individually and corporately.

[
36
]

There are a number of reasons.

[
37
]

Firstly, 121 is a foreign corporation with no
assets or presence in BC. I have no evidence before me to suggest that should
the defendant succeed in defending the plaintiffs' claim, 121, Tylon or Mr. Kretschmer
would be able to pay costs. Indeed, the evidence is to the contrary.

[
38
]

Secondly, Tylon has been struck from the register
for failure to file annual reports and does not exist.

[
39
]

Thirdly, Mr. Kretschmer has not satisfied
me that he has the ability to pay costs should this claim be dismissed. Indeed,
during submissions he admitted as much to me.

[
40
]

Fourthly, the defendant has presented a
prima
facie
case as to why security for costs should be ordered, but the
plaintiffs have not shown me why that order should not be made.

[
41
]

Fifthly, the plaintiffs make essentially three
claims against the defendant. First, they say that the defendant failed to
provide evidence of his legal fees to the plaintiffs so they could recover
those fees in their ongoing negligence claim against Mr. Rotstein. However,
the matter of Mr. Turner's legal fees is before Master Wilson, and until
Master Wilson has ruled on what those fees should be the amounts are not known.
Until the amounts are known the plaintiffs refuse to pay. In any event, it
appears from the evidence I have that the Rotstein action is in limbo and no
substantial steps have been taken by the plaintiffs to prosecute that action
since it was commenced in April 2014.

[
42
]

Next, the plaintiffs complain about Mr. Turner's
handling of the Roy claim. As indicated, Mr. Turner defended the Roy claim
for the plaintiffs in March 2011. Judgment was handed down by Justice Josephson
on April 13, 2011. Judgment was awarded against 121 for $317,300, but it was
dismissed against Mr. Kretschmer personally. The appeal of that judgment
resulted in the Court of Appeal ordering a new trial on all issues which had
the effect of starting the entire case over again. Mr. Turner was not
counsel for the plaintiffs either on the appeal or subsequently.

[
43
]

Finally, the plaintiffs complain about the
settlement in the Pont and Landon action in April 2011. The plaintiffs allege
that Mr. Turner was not ready for trial and that they were improperly forced
to settle. This issue will be very difficult to determine. It will require a
very detailed analysis and review of the background of the Pont and Landon
claims and Mr. Turner's actions or inactions, as the case may be, in
defending them. That will be a time consuming and expensive exercise. What is
not known is what the outcome would have been had those cases proceeded to
trial. What is known, however, is the outcome of the Roy action. The
circumstances involving both actions were somewhat similar. From the material
that I have in front of me, I consider the realistic chances of the plaintiffs
succeeding against the defendant on this claim as remote.

[
44
]

The plaintiffs are no strangers to the court
system, nor to applications for security for costs. They have had orders made
against them for security for costs in both this court and in the Court of
Appeal. In addition, Mr. Kretschmer has been the subject of extensive
commentary by this Court and the Court of Appeal regarding his voracity.

[
45
]

For example, in the second Roy action,
Roy v.
1216393 Ontario Inc.
,
2012 BCSC 1752
, Madam Justice Bruce stated at
paragraph 102:

… I find the
credibility of Mr. Kretschmer’s evidence in this trial to be very suspect.

[
46
]

And at paragraph 105:

Third, Mr. Kretschmer
has repeatedly blamed his lawyers for either improvident legal advice or
improper conduct as a means of avoiding responsibility for his actions. For
example, Mr. Kretschmer attempted to avoid responsibility for his decision
to cancel the contracts of the first tier purchasers by hiding behind
privileged legal opinions he received from counsel. In addition, Mr. Kretschmer
blamed his counsel in the Romfo Action for making improper admissions about his
false statements to the first tier purchasers concerning the reason for
cancelling their contracts. Lastly, Mr. Kretschmer blamed his previous
lawyer in this action for retaining documents that could have proven the
plaintiffs knew of the Adams' claim well before January 2007.

[
47
]

And in the Court of Appeal in
Roy v.
Kretschmer
,
2014 BCCA 90
, Justice Harris commented on Mr. Kretschmer's
lack of candour in respect to affidavit material filed by him in an effort to
avoid security for costs:

16.       … I am
also concerned that Mr. Kretschmer, in seeking the indulgence of the
Court, has been less than forthright with it. His lack of candour reinforces my
view that I ought not to exercise my discretion in his favour and to the
detriment of the Roys by setting aside the order. …

[
48
]

In coming to my decision and making the order I
am making, I take into account the history of this case, the many lawsuits that
have been before this Court related to the Crystal Waters development, the
findings made against Mr. Kretschmer's credibility and what I consider the
likelihood of the claims against Mr. Turner being dismissed.

[
49
]

I have reviewed the defendant's draft proposal of
costs, which are based on an estimated 15 days of trial. This case will be
document heavy and complex. It will be time consuming. It is not a
straightforward case. It is certainly not as straightforward as Mr. Kretschmer
suggests. Examinations for discovery will be lengthy. Given the plaintiffs'
apparent pattern of behaviour in prosecuting lawsuits and given the plaintiffs
have not indicated they intend to change that pattern, the 15 days estimate seems
realistic. Indeed I suspect that estimate may be conservative.

[
50
]

Therefore, for substantially the reasons set out
in Mr. MacInnis' submissions, I am granting the order sought. These will
be the orders:

1)

the plaintiffs will post security for costs for the benefit of the
defendant in the amount of $100,000 by no later than July 2, 2017;

2)

this proceeding be stayed until the plaintiffs have posted the
required security;

3)

in the event the plaintiffs fail to post the required security by
July 2, 2017, the defendant has liberty to apply to the court for a dismissal
of this action;

4)

the requirement for the plaintiffs' signatures on this order will be
dispensed with on the condition that an entered copy of this order be delivered
to the plaintiffs; and

[
51
]

I am making no order as to costs of today's
application.

“G.P. Weatherill, J.”
